title: Tell me about a disagreement you had with your manager
prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager on something that mattered. What was the disagreement, how did you handle it, and how did it resolve?
blurb: Conflict with manager (senior): can they challenge up with candor and professionalism — and handle either outcome maturely?

rubric.label: Situation & the disagreement
rubric.description: Clearly frames a substantive disagreement with their manager and why it mattered — a real difference of view, not a trivial gripe.

rubric.label: Willingness to challenge up
rubric.description: Shows they took the risk to raise the disagreement directly and respectfully, rather than staying silent or going around their manager.

rubric.label: How they handled it
rubric.description: Describes concretely how THEY approached it — private and direct, backed by reasoning or data, listening to the manager's view, focused on the issue not the person.

rubric.label: Resolution & outcome
rubric.description: Shows a mature resolution and outcome — persuaded them, met in the middle, or committed to the manager's call — with the relationship intact. Handles 'I didn't get my way' well.

rubric.label: Reflection & professionalism
rubric.description: Reflects on picking battles, respecting the manager's role and context, and what they learned about disagreeing up productively.

rubric.label: Communication & composure
rubric.description: Tells it with professionalism and no residual resentment; fair to the manager's perspective.

reference.scenario: A senior story: the candidate had a genuine, consequential disagreement with their own manager — on strategy, priorities, a people decision, an approach, or feedback about themselves — and handled it with candor and professionalism. The signal is the ability to challenge upward respectfully AND to handle the resolution maturely whether or not they got their way, keeping the relationship strong.
model_points: Situation: a substantive disagreement with their direct manager, with real stakes — not a petty complaint or a values clash dressed up.
Task: they recognized staying silent wasn't right, and took ownership of raising it directly with their manager.

Action: chose the right setting (private, direct), led with reasoning or data, framed it around the shared goal, and genuinely listened to the manager's perspective and constraints they might not have seen.
Action: kept it about the issue, not the person; disagreed without insubordination or going around/over the manager.

Result: a mature resolution — they changed the manager's mind, found a middle path, or committed fully to the manager's decision after being heard — and the working relationship stayed strong or improved.
Reflection: judgment about which disagreements are worth raising, respect for the manager's broader context and accountability, and what they learned about disagreeing up.

probes.trigger: went around or over the manager
probes.question: Did you take this to your manager directly first, or to someone else? Why?
So they made a different call than you wanted. How did you handle that, and how did you show up afterward?
Was this a professional judgment difference or something more personal? Keep it to the substance — what were the two positions?
What was your manager seeing or accountable for that you might not have had visibility into? Did that change your view?
How was your relationship with your manager afterward? Did this help or hurt your trust?

red_flags: Went around or over the manager instead of addressing it directly.
Insubordinate or disrespectful — made it personal, or refused to commit after being overruled.
Stayed silent and resents it in hindsight; never actually raised the disagreement.
Can't handle 'I didn't get my way' — bitter, undermining, or quit in a huff with no maturity.
Never considered the manager's broader context or accountability.
Trivial gripe framed as a principled stand, or badmouths the manager throughout.
follow_ups: How do you decide which disagreements with your manager are worth raising?
If your manager overruled you and you still thought they were wrong, what would you do?
How do you give your manager critical feedback about their own decisions or behavior?
How did this affect how you disagree with authority now?
reference.exemplar_answer: Situation: 'My manager wanted to pull two engineers off my team's reliability work to accelerate a feature launch. I thought it would tip us past a breaking point — our on-call load was already unsustainable — and I disagreed strongly.' Task: 'I could have just complied, but I felt I owed it to my team and to him to make the case, since he might not see the on-call data I saw daily.' Action: 'I asked for a 1:1 rather than pushing back in the group meeting. I came with data: our incident rate, on-call hours, and a projection of what deferring reliability would cost in outages during the very launch he cared about. Then I genuinely listened — he was under board pressure on the launch date I hadn't fully appreciated. So instead of a flat 'no', I proposed a middle path: move one engineer, not two, and time-box the reliability pause to four weeks with a checkpoint.' Result: 'He agreed to the compromise. The launch hit its date, we avoided a reliability blowup, and honestly the relationship got stronger — he later told me he valued that I brought data instead of just objecting. Even if he'd overruled me entirely, I'd decided going in that I'd commit once heard.' Reflection: 'I learned to challenge up by leading with the shared goal and data, in private, and to assume my manager has context I don't. I also learned to pick these moments — I don't spend that capital on small things. The maturity test isn't winning the disagreement; it's how you show up if you lose it.'

interviewer_notes: Senior bar for managing up. Two things to verify: (1) they raised it DIRECTLY with the manager, not around or over them — probe immediately if it sounds like they escalated past their manager; (2) they can handle being overruled with grace — if the manager made a different call, probe how they showed up afterward (committed vs sulked/undermined). Reward leading with data/reasoning, choosing the private setting, and genuinely engaging the manager's broader context. Distinguish a professional judgment difference from a personal/values clash. Watch tone for residual resentment or badmouthing. The signal is candor plus professionalism, not winning.
